haiku-low.q1: Keys load at startup before readiness. /healthz returns 503 until all three keys are loaded, then 200 with version ids.
haiku-low.q2: It retries the store 3 times, 2 seconds apart, then exits non-zero. It never becomes ready, the rollout halts, and old pods keep serving live traffic.
haiku-low.q3: A background task re-reads all three secrets every 5 minutes and swaps in new values. If a read fails, it keeps the last good value, logs a warning without values, and retries in 5 minutes.
haiku-low.q4: Key values live only in process memory. They must never appear on disk, in environment variables, or in logs. Version ids may be logged.
haiku-low.q5: Only the orders-api-prod identity reads prod values, read-only. Only the security on-call writes them. Engineers cannot read prod values.
haiku-low.q6: The old keys stay in git history, so they count as leaked. They become harmless only when each is revoked at its provider after rotation. The plan does not rewrite history.
haiku-low.q7: Each client calls secrets.get(name) on every request, so the next request after a refresh uses the new key.
haiku-low.q8: The operator checks each replica's /healthz shows the new version id, waiting at least 6 minutes and rechecking until all do. Only then is the old key revoked.
haiku-low.q9: Set store access, copy keys into the store, switch the app to the store and remove yaml keys in one merge, deploy and verify, then rotate keys at providers.
haiku-low.q10: make run sets APP_ENV=dev and reads orders-api/dev/* sandbox keys, using the developer's own credentials, which can read dev only.
haiku-low.q11: It counts as a failed read. The startup load retries 3 times, 2 seconds apart, then exits non-zero, so the pod never becomes ready.
haiku-low.q12: NOT STATED. The plan sets no rotation cadence, and security has not decided whether regular rotation is required.

sonnet.q1: Keys are loaded at startup first; /healthz returns 503 (not ready) until all three keys are loaded, then 200. So load happens before the pod is marked ready.
sonnet.q2: It retries 3 times 2 seconds apart, then exits non-zero and never becomes ready. The rollout halts and old pods keep serving, so live traffic is unaffected.
sonnet.q3: A background task re-reads all three secrets every 5 minutes and swaps in any new value and version id. If a read fails, it keeps the last good value, logs a warning (names and error only), and retries in 5 minutes.
sonnet.q4: Held only in process memory (value and version id). Never on disk, in environment variables, or in logs (version ids may be logged).
sonnet.q5: Read: only the orders-api-prod service identity (read-only on orders-api/prod/*). Engineers cannot read prod values. Write: only the security on-call.
sonnet.q6: The old keys remain in git history (two years), so they count as leaked; history is not being rewritten. They are made harmless by rotating every key at the provider and revoking the old ones after all replicas show the new version.
sonnet.q7: Clients no longer copy the key in constructors; each calls secrets.get(name) on every request, so the next request uses the refreshed key.
sonnet.q8: After writing the new version, wait at least 6 minutes, then check every replica's /healthz shows the new version id, repeating until all do. Revoke the old key only after that; if any replica lacks it, do not revoke.
sonnet.q9: 1) Set access policies; 2) create secrets in the store (copy keys); 3) one code merge that switches the app to the store and removes api_key from config/app.yaml (plus CI check); 4) deploy; 5) verify; 6) rotate keys at each provider one at a time; 7) update deploy.md.
sonnet.q10: From the store at orders-api/dev/* (sandbox keys), via make run with APP_ENV=dev, using the developer's own credentials, which can read dev only.
sonnet.q11: A missing secret counts as a failed read: it retries 3 times 2 seconds apart, then exits non-zero; the pod never becomes ready and the rollout halts.
sonnet.q12: NOT STATED. The rotation schedule is an open question; security has not decided and the plan sets no cadence.
